terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where tonight's report is timed step by step and its work is counted.

tasks.title: Time a function fairly
tasks.description:
Implement `timeIt(fn, runs)` in `src/measure.js`. It returns a promise of a number of milliseconds.

- it calls `fn` once first and does not time that run
- then it calls `fn` `runs` times (5 when `runs` is not given) and times each run with `performance.now()`, read just before and just after the run
- it waits for each run to finish before it reads the clock, so a `fn` that returns a promise is timed until that promise settles
- it returns the middle of those times once they are sorted from fastest to slowest; with an even number of times, the later of the two in the middle

The check never measures real time. It gives `performance.now()` a clock of its own that moves only when its own steps do work, by amounts it chose, so it knows exactly which time your function should give back.
nextSteps: Read "One run tells you little" in the lesson.
Call `fn` once before anything else, and do not keep its time.
In a loop, read `performance.now()`, wait for `fn()`, read it again, and keep the difference.
Sort the times and give back the one in the middle.
hints: Three things decide the answer: which runs are timed, how each run is timed, and which of the times you give back.

The first run of a function is often slower: the engine has not yet turned it into fast code. Leave that run out. Of the rest, the time in the middle of the sorted list says what a usual run takes; one slow run cannot pull it up the way it pulls up an average.
`await fn()`, then for each run: `const start = performance.now(); await fn(); times.push(performance.now() - start)`. Then `times.sort((a, b) => a - b)` and return `times[Math.floor(runs / 2)]`.

tasks.title: Find the slow step
tasks.description:
Implement `timeSteps(steps, runs)` in `src/measure.js`. `steps` is an object whose values are functions, such as `{ match, money, print }`. It returns a promise of a list.

- it times each step with your `timeIt(step, runs)`, one step after another, never two at the same time
- `runs` is passed on to `timeIt`; when it is not given, `timeIt` gets 5
- the list has one `{ name, ms }` per step: the step's name in the object, and the time `timeIt` gave for it
- the slowest step comes first

The check uses steps of its own whose costs it chose on its own clock, and reads the names and times in your list.
nextSteps: Run `node src/try.js`: task 1 times the match step alone.
Go through the steps with `Object.entries` and time each one with `timeIt`, waiting for one before the next.
Keep a `{ name, ms }` for each.
Sort the list so the slowest comes first, and run the script again.
hints: The report has three steps of work. Before you change any of them, you want to know which one the night goes on.

`Object.entries(steps)` gives `[name, fn]` pairs. Timing them all at once with `Promise.all` lets their runs overlap, and then each time takes in the others: wait for each step's time before starting the next.
`for (const [name, step] of Object.entries(steps)) timed.push({ name, ms: await timeIt(step, runs) })`, then `timed.sort((a, b) => b.ms - a.ms)`.

tasks.title: Count the work
tasks.description:
Implement `counted(fn)` in `src/measure.js`. It returns a new function.

- the new function calls `fn` with all the arguments it was given and returns exactly what `fn` returns
- it has a property `calls`: 0 at first, and one more after each call
- when `fn` throws, the error reaches the caller, and the call still counts
- two counted functions keep two separate counts

The check counts the comparisons of a sort with it, calls it with several arguments, makes two at once, and wraps a function that throws.
nextSteps: Read "Counting, which no computer changes" in the lesson.
Write a function inside `counted` that adds one to its own count and then calls `fn`.
Give that function a `calls` property that starts at 0.
Run `node src/try.js` and read what task 3 counts.
hints: A function is an object, so it can carry a property of its own, and code inside it can reach that function by name.
Write a named function inside `counted`, with rest parameters `...args` to take any number of arguments. Each call of `counted` makes a new one, so each has its own count.
`function wrapped(...args) { wrapped.calls += 1; return fn(...args) }`, then `wrapped.calls = 0` and `return wrapped`.
